scenes.title: Two Natural Causes
scenes.summary: Imitation is natural to us from childhood, the way we first learn, and everyone delights in imitations, even of things painful to see, because learning is a pleasure.

scenes.title: From Improvisation to Poetry
scenes.summary: Since imitation, melody and rhythm come by nature, the gifted advanced little by little and made poetry out of their improvisations.

scenes.title: Hymns and Invectives
scenes.summary: Poetry split by the poets' characters: the dignified imitated noble actions in hymns and encomia, the trivial mean ones in invectives, and the iambic meter came in with the Margites.

scenes.title: Homer, Master of Both
scenes.summary: Homer was the poet of serious things and of dramatic imitation, and showed the form of comedy too: the Margites is to comedy what the Iliad and the Odyssey are to tragedy.

scenes.title: Comedy and Tragedy Appear
scenes.summary: Poets turned from lampoon to comedy and from epic to tragedy, as to the greater forms; whether tragedy is fully developed is another question.

scenes.title: From the Dithyramb and the Phallic Songs
scenes.summary: Tragedy grew from those who led the dithyramb, comedy from the phallic songs, until tragedy found its nature and stopped.

scenes.title: Actors, Scene Painting, Meter
scenes.summary: Aeschylus raised the actors to two and gave speech the lead; Sophocles added a third and scene painting; tragedy grew out of the satyric into dignity, the iambic replaced the tetrameter, and the episodes multiplied.
